A persistent higher differential pressure supports restriction; a fluid contamination test addresses a different failure mode, cross-leakage.
example.result: Plan inspection and cleaning using the maker's isolation, plate sequence and tightening instructions. Do not assume every temperature rise requires a new plate pack.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: In a shell-and-tube exchanger, one fluid flows through tubes and the other around them. Baffles guide shell-side flow, but also affect pressure drop. Tube leakage can mix fluids in the direction set by their local pressure difference, which may change when pumps stop.

example.problem: Cooling water contamination appears after shutdown although normal running samples are clean. How could a tube leak explain this?
steps: Compare pressures during running and shutdown; their ordering may reverse.
An isolated pressure or leak test can identify a damaged boundary without assuming the normal running flow direction persists.
example.result: A leak path and a pressure difference together determine contamination direction. Follow an approved test pressure and isolation procedure; excessive test pressure can damage sound tubes.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Fouling adds thermal resistance, but its symptoms overlap with low flow, air binding and changed seawater temperature. Compare an exchanger against a clean baseline at similar duty and flow before deciding that cleaning is the remedy. A single outlet temperature is insufficient evidence.

example.problem: At the same flow and inlet temperatures, a cooler transfers 80 kW instead of its previous 100 kW, and water-side pressure drop has increased.
steps: Estimate heat duty from mass flow, heat capacity and measured temperature change.
The combined thermal and hydraulic changes strengthen the restriction hypothesis; verify instrument accuracy and strainers before opening the exchanger.
example.result: Record performance again after cleaning. Recovery toward the baseline demonstrates the effect of the intervention; lack of recovery directs investigation toward another cause.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Heat exchanger effectiveness compares actual heat transfer with the maximum possible for the inlet temperatures and smaller heat-capacity rate. It differs from thermal efficiency of an engine. The smaller capacity rate sets the maximum because that stream would otherwise cross the opposite inlet temperature.

example.problem: Hot and cold capacity rates are 4 and 2 kW/K. Inlet temperatures are 80°C and 20°C; measured duty is 90 kW.
steps: Maximum duty is Cmin(Th,in − Tc,in) = 2 × 60 = 120 kW.
Effectiveness is 90/120 = 0.75. Cold outlet temperature is 20 + 90/2 = 65°C.
example.result: The effectiveness is 75%, with hot outlet 57.5°C. This temperature pattern requires a compatible flow arrangement; energy balance should agree on both sides within measurement uncertainty.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: An exhaust economizer transfers exhaust heat into water or steam. Soot deposits both resist heat transfer and can become combustible. A declining steam output is therefore a performance clue, while abnormal gas temperatures or fire indications demand the vessel's emergency response rather than routine cleaning.

example.problem: Steam production drops at the same engine load while gas-side pressure drop rises. What should the engineer investigate?
steps: Compare exhaust inlet conditions, feedwater flow and instrumentation with the clean baseline.
Examine approved soot-cleaning history and restrictions without treating a possible soot fire as an ordinary fouling problem.
example.result: Assess cleaning under the maker's procedure and safe operating conditions. Never improvise water application to a hot economizer; distinguish preventive cleaning from the specific fire response.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Waste heat recovery converts part of otherwise rejected energy into useful heating or power. Gross recovered output can overstate the benefit if additional pumps, fans or exhaust backpressure increase fuel use. The useful comparison is the net change at an equivalent ship operating condition.

example.problem: A recovery unit generates 180 kW while its new auxiliaries consume 25 kW. What benefit can be claimed from these figures alone?
steps: Subtract auxiliary consumption: preliminary net electrical output is 155 kW.
Check any added engine fuel consumption or propulsion penalty before converting this into a voyage fuel saving.
example.result: 155 kW is a subsystem result, not yet a complete ship saving. Include availability, low-load performance and whether recovered heat replaces a real demand.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: A steam turbine converts an enthalpy drop into shaft work. Available power depends on steam mass flow, inlet state, exhaust pressure and actual turbine efficiency. Supplying a turbine must not compromise essential steam consumers or boiler water level control.

example.problem: Steam flow is 0.5 kg/s and the ideal available enthalpy drop is 400 kJ/kg. Assume turbine efficiency 70% and neglect generator losses.
steps: Ideal shaft power is 0.5 × 400 = 200 kW.
Actual shaft power is approximately 0.70 × 200 = 140 kW under these assumptions.
example.result: Electrical output will be lower after generator and auxiliary losses. Verify steam quality and operating limits; a calculated power figure does not establish safe turbine admission conditions.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Cogeneration produces useful heat and power from the same fuel input. Its reported total efficiency depends on counting heat that is actually used. Dumping excess hot water overboard does not create an energy-saving credit, even if the recovery equipment is available.

example.problem: A plant consumes 1000 kW of fuel energy, produces 350 kW electricity and supplies 400 kW of useful heating.
steps: Electrical efficiency is 35%; useful combined efficiency is (350 + 400)/1000 = 75%.
If heating demand falls to 100 kW, useful combined efficiency becomes 45%, although electrical output is unchanged.
example.result: Compare operation over the real demand profile. Match recovery capacity to consumers and avoid presenting installed heat-recovery capacity as continuous useful output.

topicTitle: Enerji dönüşüm verimi ve kayıp analizi

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: An energy balance follows energy into useful output, rejected heat and other losses. Successive conversion efficiencies multiply rather than add. Define the system boundary first so that auxiliaries or electrical losses are not counted twice or silently omitted.

example.problem: An engine converts 40% of fuel energy to shaft work and its generator converts 95% of shaft work to electricity. Fuel input is 1000 kW.
steps: Shaft output is 400 kW; generator output is 400 × 0.95 = 380 kW.
Overall conversion efficiency is 0.40 × 0.95 = 38%, before external auxiliaries.
example.result: The remaining 620 kW leaves through heat and other losses. A useful loss analysis assigns each stream to the same boundary and operating condition before selecting an improvement.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Heading describes the bow direction; course over ground describes displacement over the seabed. Leeway can also separate heading from the through-water velocity, so a current triangle that ignores wind is a simplified model. Compare instruments using the same true or magnetic reference and time interval.

example.problem: A vessel makes 10 kn north through the water while a 2 kn current sets east. Assume no leeway. Find the ground track.
steps: Resolve north and east components: 10 kn north and 2 kn east.
The angle east of north is arctan(2/10) = 11.3 degrees; ground speed is sqrt(104) = 10.20 kn.
example.result: Heading 000°T produces COG approximately 011°T. To maintain a northward track, steer into the current and recompute the triangle; do not simply substitute COG for heading.

section.title: Apply the principle
section.content: Speed through water measures motion relative to the surrounding water; speed over ground measures motion relative to the seabed. They are vector magnitudes. Subtracting the two scalar readings gives current speed only when the velocities lie on the same line. A cross-current can increase SOG while also creating an unwanted track offset.

example.problem: The ship maintains 12 kn through water on an eastward heading. Compare a 3 kn following current with a 3 kn current setting north.
steps: With the following current, eastward ground speed is 12 + 3 = 15 kn.
With the cross-current, SOG is sqrt(12² + 3²) = 12.37 kn and COG turns 14.0 degrees north of east.
example.result: The same current speed gives different SOG and track. Use SOG for distance-over-ground estimates, but retain STW and current direction when evaluating propulsion performance or predicting the vessel's path.
